vjimc-2018-cat2-01.title: Mean value theorem on $t^x$
vjimc-2018-cat2-01.body:
Rewrite the equation as $17^x-11^x=8^x-2^x$. Clearly $x=0$ and $x=1$ are solutions: $2=2$ and $19=19$.

Let $x\ne0$ be a solution and $\varphi(t)=t^x$. By the mean value theorem there are $t_1\in(2,8)$ and $t_2\in(11,17)$ with
$$8^x-2^x=6\varphi'(t_1)=6x\,t_1^{x-1},\qquad 17^x-11^x=6\varphi'(t_2)=6x\,t_2^{x-1}.$$
Hence $x\,t_1^{x-1}=x\,t_2^{x-1}$, and since $x\ne0$, $(t_2/t_1)^{x-1}=1$. Because $t_2>t_1$, this forces $x=1$.

**Answer: $x=0$ or $x=1$.** ∎

vjimc-2018-cat2-01.title: Strict convexity (Karamata)
vjimc-2018-cat2-01.body:
Note $2+17=8+11$ and $2<8<11<17$. Write
$$8=\tfrac35\cdot2+\tfrac25\cdot17,\qquad11=\tfrac25\cdot2+\tfrac35\cdot17 .$$
For $x<0$ or $x>1$ the function $\varphi(t)=t^x$ is strictly convex on $(0,\infty)$, since $\varphi''=x(x-1)t^{x-2}>0$. Then
$$\varphi(8)+\varphi(11)<\big(\tfrac35+\tfrac25\big)\varphi(2)+\big(\tfrac25+\tfrac35\big)\varphi(17)=\varphi(2)+\varphi(17),$$
i.e. $8^x+11^x<2^x+17^x$. For $0<x<1$, $\varphi$ is strictly concave and the inequality reverses. So there are no solutions except $x=0$ and $x=1$, where $\varphi$ is affine and equality holds. **Answer: $x\in\{0,1\}$.** ∎

vjimc-2018-cat2-02.title: Induction (official)
vjimc-2018-cat2-02.body:
We use $[u]+[v]\le[u+v]$, which holds because $[u]+[v]$ is an integer $\le u+v$.

Induction on $n$. For $n=1$ the condition gives $a_1=0$ and the claim is trivial.

Assume the statement for $n$, and let $a_1\le\dots\le a_{n+1}$ with $\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}ia_i=0$. Then $a_{n+1}\ge0$: otherwise all $a_i<0$ and the weighted sum would be negative. Put $b_i=a_i+\frac{2a_{n+1}}n$ for $i\le n$. The $b_i$ are still nondecreasing, and
$$\sum_{i=1}^nib_i=\sum_{i=1}^nia_i+\frac{2a_{n+1}}n\cdot\frac{n(n+1)}2=\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}ia_i=0 .$$
By the induction hypothesis,
$$0\le\sum_{i=1}^nb_i[ix]=\sum_{i=1}^na_i[ix]+a_{n+1}\cdot\frac2n\sum_{i=1}^n[ix].$$
Summing $[ix]+[(n+1-i)x]\le[(n+1)x]$ over $i=1,\dots,n$ gives $\frac2n\sum_{i=1}^n[ix]\le[(n+1)x]$. Since $a_{n+1}\ge0$,
$$0\le\sum_{i=1}^na_i[ix]+a_{n+1}[(n+1)x]=\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}a_i[ix].\ ∎$$

vjimc-2018-cat2-02.title: Abel summation
vjimc-2018-cat2-02.body:
Let $P_k=\sum_{j=1}^k[jx]$. Summing $[jx]+[(k-j)x]\le[kx]$ over $j=1,\dots,k-1$ gives $2P_{k-1}\le(k-1)[kx]=(k-1)(P_k-P_{k-1})$. Hence $(k+1)P_{k-1}\le(k-1)P_k$, i.e.
$$\frac{P_{k-1}}{(k-1)k}\le\frac{P_k}{k(k+1)} .$$
So $\frac{P_k}{k(k+1)}$ is nondecreasing in $k$.

Let $\tau=\frac{2P_n}{n(n+1)}$, $w_i=[ix]-\tau i$ and $W_k=\sum_{i\le k}w_i=P_k-\tau\frac{k(k+1)}2$. Then $W_n=0$, and by monotonicity $W_k=\frac{k(k+1)}2\Big(\frac{2P_k}{k(k+1)}-\frac{2P_n}{n(n+1)}\Big)\le0$. Since $\sum ia_i=0$, Abel summation gives
$$\sum_{i=1}^na_i[ix]=\sum_{i=1}^na_iw_i=a_nW_n-\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}(a_{k+1}-a_k)W_k=-\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}(a_{k+1}-a_k)W_k\ge0,$$
because $a_{k+1}-a_k\ge0$ and $W_k\le0$. ∎

vjimc-2018-cat2-03.title: Cubic surfaces and six planes
vjimc-2018-cat2-03.body:
**Lower bound $n\ge20$.** The polynomials in $x,y,z$ of degree at most $3$ form a vector space of dimension $\binom{6}{3}=20$. If $n\le19$, the $n$ linear conditions $p(A)=0$ (for the coloured points $A$) have a nonzero solution $p$.

Every point Vojtěch can colour is also a zero of $p$. Indeed, if $p$ vanishes at four distinct points of a line $\{A+tv\}$, then $t\mapsto p(A+tv)$ is a polynomial of degree $\le3$ in $t$ with four roots, hence identically zero. So $p$ vanishes on the whole line. But a nonzero polynomial does not vanish everywhere in $\mathbb R^3$, so some point can never be coloured.

**Construction with $20$ points.** Take six planes $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_6$ in general position:
* any two meet in a line $\ell_{ij}=\alpha_i\cap\alpha_j$;
* any three meet in exactly one point;
* no four share a point.

Colour the $\binom63=20$ triple points $\alpha_i\cap\alpha_j\cap\alpha_k$.

1. **Each line $\ell_{ij}$:** it contains the four distinct triple points $\alpha_i\cap\alpha_j\cap\alpha_k$, $k\ne i,j$, so every point of $\ell_{ij}$ can be coloured.
2. **Each plane $\alpha_i$:** let $P\in\alpha_i$ not lie on any $\ell_{ij}$. Choose a line $m\subset\alpha_i$ through $P$ that is not parallel to any of the five lines $\ell_{ij}$ ($j\ne i$) and avoids the finitely many triple points in $\alpha_i$. Then $m$ meets the five lines in five distinct points. They are distinct because two of them coinciding would be a triple point. All five can be coloured by step 1, so $P$ can be coloured.
3. **Any point $P$:** if $P$ lies on some $\alpha_i$, use step 2. Otherwise choose a line through $P$ that is not parallel to any $\alpha_i$ and meets none of the fifteen lines $\ell_{ij}$; this excludes finitely many planes of directions. It meets the six planes in six distinct points, which can be coloured by step 2, so $P$ can be coloured.

Hence $20$ points suffice, and the minimum is $n=20$. **Answer: 20.** ∎

vjimc-2018-cat2-04.title: Differentiate with respect to a parameter (official)
vjimc-2018-cat2-04.body:
For $0\le\varrho\le1$ let
$$F(\varrho)=\iint_{\mathbb R^2}\Big(\frac{1-e^{-\varrho xy}}{xy}\Big)^2e^{-x^2-y^2}dx\,dy$$
(the integrand is continuous, with value $\varrho^2e^{-x^2-y^2}$ where $xy=0$). We need $F(1)$.

**A Gaussian integral.** For $|t|<1$, complete the square:
$$\iint e^{-x^2-2txy-y^2}dx\,dy=\iint e^{-(x+ty)^2-(1-t^2)y^2}dx\,dy=\sqrt\pi\cdot\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{1-t^2}}=\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{1-t^2}} .$$

**Derivatives.** Let $f$ be the integrand. Then
$$\partial_\varrho f=\frac{2e^{-\varrho xy}-2e^{-2\varrho xy}}{xy}e^{-x^2-y^2},\qquad\partial_\varrho^2f=\big(4e^{-2\varrho xy}-2e^{-\varrho xy}\big)e^{-x^2-y^2}.$$
For $0\le\varrho\le1-\varepsilon$, we have $2\varrho|xy|\le\varrho(x^2+y^2)$, so
$$|\partial^2_\varrho f|\le6e^{2\varrho|xy|-x^2-y^2}\le6e^{-\varepsilon(x^2+y^2)},$$
which is integrable. Also $f$ and $\partial_\varrho f$ vanish at $\varrho=0$, so they are bounded by the same function. Hence we may differentiate under the integral sign on $[0,1)$. Using the Gaussian integral with $t=\varrho$ and $t=\varrho/2$,
$$F''(\varrho)=\frac{4\pi}{\sqrt{1-\varrho^2}}-\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{1-\varrho^2/4}} .$$
Since $F'(0)=F(0)=0$,
$$F'(\varrho)=4\pi\arcsin\varrho-4\pi\arcsin\frac\varrho2 ,$$
$$F(\varrho)=4\pi\Big[\varrho\arcsin\varrho+\sqrt{1-\varrho^2}-1-\varrho\arcsin\frac\varrho2-\sqrt{4-\varrho^2}+2\Big].$$

**Passing to $\varrho=1$.** For every fixed $u=xy$, the function $\varrho\mapsto\frac{1-e^{-\varrho u}}u$ is nonnegative and nondecreasing on $[0,1]$: its $\varrho$-derivative is $e^{-\varrho u}>0$. So the integrand increases with $\varrho$, and by the monotone convergence theorem $F(1)=\lim_{\varrho\to1^-}F(\varrho)$. Hence
$$F(1)=4\pi\Big[\frac\pi2-1-\frac\pi6-\sqrt3+2\Big]=\frac{4\pi^2}3-4(\sqrt3-1)\pi\approx3.9603 .$$
**Answer: $\frac{4\pi^2}{3}-4(\sqrt3-1)\pi$.**

vjimc-2018-cat2-04.title: Write the square as a double integral
vjimc-2018-cat2-04.body:
For every real $u$,
$$\Big(\frac{1-e^{-u}}u\Big)^2=\Big(\int_0^1e^{-us}ds\Big)^2=\int_0^1\!\!\int_0^1e^{-u(s+t)}\,ds\,dt$$
(for $u=0$ both sides equal $1$). Put $u=xy$ and integrate over $\mathbb R^2$. Everything is nonnegative, so Tonelli's theorem lets us swap the integrals. Using the Gaussian integral $\iint e^{-x^2-2\tau xy-y^2}=\frac\pi{\sqrt{1-\tau^2}}$ with $\tau=\frac{s+t}2<1$ (for almost every $(s,t)$):
$$I=\int_0^1\!\!\int_0^1\frac{\pi\,ds\,dt}{\sqrt{1-\frac{(s+t)^2}4}} .$$
The sum $w=s+t$ of the two coordinates has density $w$ on $[0,1]$ and $2-w$ on $[1,2]$. Hence
$$I=\pi\int_0^1\frac{w\,dw}{\sqrt{1-w^2/4}}+\pi\int_1^2\frac{(2-w)\,dw}{\sqrt{1-w^2/4}} .$$
Since $\int\frac{w\,dw}{\sqrt{1-w^2/4}}=-4\sqrt{1-w^2/4}$ and $\int\frac{dw}{\sqrt{1-w^2/4}}=2\arcsin\frac w2$:
* the first integral is $4-2\sqrt3$;
* the second is $4\big(\frac\pi2-\frac\pi6\big)-2\sqrt3=\frac{4\pi}3-2\sqrt3$.

So
$$I=\pi\Big(\frac{4\pi}3+4-4\sqrt3\Big)=\frac{4\pi^2}3-4(\sqrt3-1)\pi\approx3.96025,$$
which agrees with a direct numerical evaluation. ∎
